name: ai-kernel-optimizer
baseline: GCC -O3 compiled C reference kernels (scalar 256-byte-LUT base64 decode, LZ4 1.10.0 fast-path decode, Redis 7.x SipHash 1-2)
workload: Differential-fuzzed x86-64 assembly replacements, written by an AI model and driven by optimize.py, for three extracted kernels; base64 decode timed at 64 B, 1 KiB and 16 KiB inputs, LZ4 fast-path decode on 4096-byte blocks, SipHash on 8-byte and 32-byte keys.
claimed_speedup: Base64 decode 4.80x (64 B: 1,767 to 8,479 MB/s), 6.23x (1 KiB: 1,825 to 11,365 MB/s), 6.26x (16 KiB: 1,857 to 11,635 MB/s) over GCC -O3; LZ4 fast-path decode about 1.02-1.07x (author says within noise); Redis SipHash 0.97x (GCC about 3% faster).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native (per the repo's blog post; GCC version not stated)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only, SSSE3 for the base64 kernel (BMI2 rorx in the SipHash attempt). The base64 kernel assumes valid input, no padding characters and a length that is a multiple of 4, so it skips the error handling a production decoder needs. Base64 code is about twice the size of GCC's (293 vs 145 bytes). The tool only handles pure kernels with no I/O, allocation or global state; the full LZ4_decompress_safe (856 instructions) was too large, so only its fast path was replaced.
caveats: All numbers are self-reported in case_studies/*/REPORT.md and the blog post. The REPORT.md files list the C reference, the .S assembly, harness.c and build_and_test.sh, but the repo does not contain them (raw.githubusercontent.com returns 404 for case_studies/base64/b64_decode_kern.c, harness.c, b64_decode_kern_ai.S and build_and_test.sh), so nothing can be rerun. CPU model and GCC version are not stated and timing method (warmup, repeats) is not described. The baseline is a scalar LUT decoder; the base64 win comes from a different algorithm (pshufb nibble lookup), and existing SIMD base64 libraries (aklomp/base64, fastbase64, simdutf) were not compared. The README's 'provably outperforms GCC -O3' is overstated: verification is 100K differential-fuzz iterations per kernel, and the tool's own results include a loss (SipHash) and a within-noise tie (LZ4). Hacker News thread itself could not be opened (egress blocked).
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch 'Show HN assembler faster than GNU as' (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) surfaced Show HN 'AI-optimized x86-64 assembly vs. GCC -O3 on three production kernels' (HN item 47021641); an extended WebSearch on that title led to the repo, then github.com pages and raw files were opened.

name: CryptOpt
baseline: GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 at -O3 compiling the Fiat Cryptography C for the same field operations; also hand-optimized assembly in libsecp256k1
workload: Multiply and square for the finite fields of Curve25519, P-224, P-256, P-384, P-521, Curve448, secp256k1, SIKEp434 and Poly1305, with x86-64 assembly found by randomized program search on each target CPU and checked for equivalence against the Fiat IR in Coq, measured on ten x86-64 machines.
claimed_speedup: Mean 1.74x over GCC 12.1.0 and 1.40x over Clang 15.0.6 across ten x86-64 platforms (paper text). Geometric means by function (Clang / GCC): P-256 multiply 1.70 / 2.61, P-224 multiply 1.54 / 2.52, secp256k1 multiply 1.80 / 2.62, SIKEp434 multiply 1.70 / 2.43, Curve25519 multiply 1.25 / 1.16, Poly1305 multiply 1.12 / 1.22; Curve448 multiply 1.19 / 0.98 and P-521 multiply 1.30 / 0.97 (slower than GCC). Average 1.04x over the hand-optimized libsecp256k1 assembly.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline: GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 with -march=native -mtune=native -O3 (highest optimization level); CPU frequency fixed and boosting disabled; Ubuntu Server 22.04.1 on all machines
hardware: Ten x86-64 machines from the paper's Table 1: AMD Ryzen 1900X (Zen 1), Ryzen 7 5800X and Ryzen 9 5950X (Zen 3), Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4); Intel Core i7-6770HQ (Skylake-H), i7-10710U (Comet Lake-U), i9-10900K (Comet Lake-S), i7-11700KF (Rocket Lake-S), i9-12900KF (Alder Lake-S), i9-13900KF (Raptor Lake-S)
stars_or_usage: 73 stars; generated assembly is merged into Fiat Cryptography's fiat-amd64 directory
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and specific to straight-line field-arithmetic functions; the search is run on each target CPU and the best result is kept, so gains vary by microarchitecture. Big functions (Curve448 and P-521 multiply, 500-650 instructions) get no gain over GCC. The equivalence checker needs Fiat IR; the libsecp256k1 comparison (1.04x) could not be equivalence-checked. Needs Node.js and the optimizer's own measuring run per machine.
caveats: Baseline is compiler output on Fiat's generated C, not an assembler; the category fit is as an assembly-generating tool. Speedups are geometric means over platforms, and per-platform results are in the arXiv full version and the zenodo artifact (both unreachable here, only the in-repo PLDI PDF and README table were opened). Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper; it would be A if a verifier confirms the repo or zenodo artifact reruns the GCC/Clang comparison (paper states CPUs, compilers and flags). Last commit is November 2023. Also surfaced by the w13-asm-papers search under hand-written-asm-kernels.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch 'Hacker News superoptimizer assembly tool faster code than GCC LLVM github show hn' (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) returned only older superoptimizer threads (STOKE, Learning to Superoptimize); CryptOpt itself was chosen from prior knowledge of superoptimizer literature and opened on github.com and via its in-repo paper, not from an HN thread.
